sources.title: The Practical Test Pyramid (Ham Vocke)
findings: Keep two things from Cohn's pyramid: write tests of different granularity, and the higher the level the fewer tests; lots of small fast unit tests, some coarser tests, very few end-to-end tests.
Warns against the test ice-cream cone (mostly high-level tests), which is slow and hard to maintain; the layer names are less important than the granularity.
sources.limits: Practitioner article; examples are Java and Spring.

sources.title: The Testing Trophy and Testing Classifications (Kent C. Dodds)
findings: Trophy layers from bottom to top: static analysis, unit, integration, end to end, as a guide to the return on investment of each form of testing.
Guiding principle: the more tests resemble the way the software is used, the more confidence they give.
sources.limits: Framed for JavaScript applications; publication date read from the page.

sources.title: Test Sizes (Simon Stewart, Google Testing Blog)
findings: Small tests use no network, database, file system, external systems, threads, or sleeps and finish within 60 seconds; medium tests may use localhost, a database, files, and sleeps within 300 seconds; large tests may use anything, 900 seconds and more.
Sizes are defined by measurable resources, so a harness can enforce them, unlike the names unit, integration, and end to end.
sources.limits: 2010 post; Google's current limits may differ.

sources.title: Pact documentation: Introduction
findings: Pact is a code-first consumer-driven contract testing tool: the contract is generated by the consumer's tests and verified against the provider, so only behavior consumers use is pinned.
A Pact contract is contract by example, a set of concrete request and response pairs, unlike a static schema such as OpenAPI.
sources.limits: Tool documentation; the page also advertises a commercial service.

sources.title: What is mutation testing? (Stryker Mutator)
findings: Mutation testing applies small changes (mutants) to the code one at a time and runs the tests; a mutant is killed when a test fails and survives when none does.
A surviving mutant points at a missing test, for example no test for an age below the boundary.
sources.limits: Tool documentation for StrykerJS, Stryker4s, and Stryker.NET.

sources.title: Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests (Martin Fowler)
findings: Quarantine non-deterministic tests in a separate suite so the healthy suite keeps its signal, and bound the quarantine by count or time so tests are fixed, not forgotten.
Never use bare sleeps to wait for asynchronous responses; use a callback or polling with a timeout.
sources.limits: Essay; causes and fixes argued from experience.

sources.title: Testing Implementation Details (Kent C. Dodds)
findings: Tests of implementation details give false negatives (break on a refactor) and false positives (pass while the application is broken).
sources.limits: Examples are React components; publication date read from the page.

sources.title: Test Coverage (Martin Fowler)
findings: Coverage is a useful tool for finding untested code and of little use as a numeric statement of test quality.
A coverage target invites low-quality tests up to assertion-free testing; quoting Brian Marick: expect a high level of coverage, do not require one.

sources.title: Software Engineering at Google, chapter 11: Testing Overview
findings: Beyonce Rule: test everything you do not want to break, including failure handling, performance, accessibility, and security.

Anti-patterns: the ice cream cone (mostly end-to-end and manual tests) and the hourglass (many unit and end-to-end, few integration tests, caused by tight coupling); the right mix depends on local architecture and organization.
A coverage bar such as 80 percent turns from a floor into a ceiling; judge which behaviors are tested instead.
sources.limits: Google-scale practice; Google's own mix is one data point, not a norm.

sources.title: Software Engineering at Google, chapter 13: Test Doubles
findings: Prefer realism over isolation: use the real implementation when it is fast, deterministic, and simple to build; otherwise prefer a fake, then a stub or mock.
Prefer state testing over interaction testing; interaction tests cannot show the result is right and break on refactors.
Non-hermetic dependencies (external services, the system clock) make tests nondeterministic; use a double or a hermetic instance.
